title: Scenario 1 knowledge check
notes: PROVISIONAL INSTRUMENT. Revised 2026-10-28 so every item tests real farming knowledge that the game and its feedback actually teach, in plain language for smallholder farmers. Still needs supervisor review before any study use. Editing this file is enough to change the instrument - no code changes are required. Baseline maize season: prepare the seedbed, sow, keep the crop out of water stress, harvest at maturity.

questions.text: This season, seed would only go into tilled ground. On a real farm, what does a well-prepared seedbed do for maize?
options: It feeds the crop, so less fertiliser is needed
It keeps the seed dry until the rains come
It helps the seed sprout evenly and the roots grow down quickly
Nothing much - seed grows just as well in hard ground
questions.explanation: Seed in loose, moist soil sprouts at the same time and gets its roots down fast, so the crop comes up even and can reach water deeper in the soil. In hard ground seed sprouts patchily and roots stay shallow, so the plants dry out sooner.

questions.text: Maize that is kept a bit too dry for weeks - but never wilts badly - will usually:
options: Grow more slowly and give a smaller harvest
Be fine, because it never wilted
Grow deeper roots and give a bigger harvest
Lose a few leaves, but the cobs are not affected
questions.explanation: A crop does not have to wilt to lose yield. Even mild dryness slows growth, and over weeks that adds up to smaller cobs. You saw the same thing in the game: tiles that were 'drying out' grew more slowly than well-watered ones.

questions.text: How do you know maize grown for grain is ready to harvest?
options: As soon as the silks (the hair on the cob) appear
When the cobs are full size but the husks are still green
When the bottom leaves of the plant start to turn yellow
When the husks are dry and brown and the kernels are hard
questions.explanation: Grain maize is mature when the husks have dried and the kernels are hard - a small black layer forms where each kernel joins the cob. Harvested too early, the grain is soft and spoils in storage. Left too long, it is open to birds, rats, insects and rot, so bring it in once it is ready.
